When the price of a loaf and a pint of milk goes up by a few pence, a household with a comfortable margin absorbs it without noticing. A household with no margin at all absorbs it by eating less, or by turning the heating off, or by falling behind on the rent. That is the distributional reality of inflation, and it is why the standard reassurance that price rises are transitory is so hollow to the people I represent. Transitory over what horizon? A family does not get to average its hunger over eighteen months.

There are three things the Government could do now. First, uprate benefits and pensions in line with the actual inflation people face, not a lagged figure taken from a month when prices happened to be lower. The lag in the uprating mechanism is quietly taking money out of the pockets of those least able to lose it. Second, act on energy specifically. The price cap has become a mechanism for passing wholesale volatility straight through to consumers with a short delay, and the social tariff that used to protect the most vulnerable has withered. Third, look seriously at housing costs, because local housing allowance has been frozen while private rents have climbed, and the gap is now met out of money meant for food.

I accept that no Government controls global gas prices. I accept that supply chains are recovering unevenly from the pandemic. But the choice about who bears the cost of that adjustment is entirely a political choice, and at the moment it is being made in favour of those who can bear it least.

That is precisely why the guidance accompanying the regime matters as much as the statutory text itself. Public authorities are not, in the main, seeking to evade their obligations. They are seeking to understand them, and they are working with finite legal capacity, particularly at local authority level, where a single solicitor may be advising across a dozen unrelated statutory schemes. If we write duties that can only be interpreted with the benefit of counsel's opinion, we will get inconsistent application, and the inconsistency will fall hardest on the beneficiaries who have the least capacity to challenge it.

So I want to give the House three assurances. First, the guidance will be published in draft, and consulted on, before the duties are commenced, so that authorities have a settled understanding before they are held to account against it. Second, we will provide a transition period of sufficient length for authorities to adjust their internal processes, their record keeping and their staff training. Third, we will monitor compliance actively rather than waiting for litigation to reveal failures. Litigation is a poor regulatory instrument. It is slow, it is expensive, it depends on someone having the resources and the tenacity to bring a case, and by the time it concludes the person who was wronged has often moved on or given up.

I say to the honourable Member who raised the point about enforcement that I do not regard the prospect of judicial review as a substitute for a proper compliance framework. It is a backstop, and a backstop that we should hope never to need. What I want is a regime in which the duty is clear, the expectation is understood, the resources are adequate, and the beneficiary receives what Parliament intended without having to fight for it.

On the question of resourcing, I say to the House that a right of access is only as real as the capacity of the body to respond. Where decision-makers are handling substantial volumes alongside their substantive duties, delay is inevitable, and delayed information is often information rendered useless. The review will consider the resourcing model as well as the legislative framework.

The difficulty is that the advice was framed as a request to employers rather than as a protection for employees. If an employer is told to consider whether staff should travel, and the employer considers it and decides that they should, the worker has no recourse. They are left choosing between their safety and their shift. For workers in secure employment with an understanding manager, that is an inconvenience. For workers on insecure contracts, in retail, in hospitality, in contract cleaning, in care, it is not a choice at all. If they do not turn up, they do not get paid, and in some cases they do not get called back.

I want to ask the Minister three specific things. First, will she consider whether the status of a red alert should carry a defined legal effect for employment purposes, so that a worker who does not travel during a red alert is protected from any detriment? Second, will she engage with the transport operators about the sequencing of announcements, because a shutdown announced at seven in the morning strands people who left home at half six? Third, what is being done for workers in essential services who must travel, in terms of transport provision and accommodation?

We were fortunate on this occasion. The forecasting was accurate, the emergency services were well prepared, and the loss of life was far lower than it might have been. But we should not build our resilience on good fortune, and we should not build it on the assumption that every employer will do the right thing.

Let me put some of this in concrete terms. In my constituency office last week I met a woman in her fifties who has worked in the same job for twenty-two years, who has never missed a rent payment, and who has been served notice because the property is being sold. There is nothing in the current framework that helps her. She earns too much for social housing, too little for a mortgage on anything within an hour of her work, and the rents she is being quoted for a replacement are three hundred euro a month above what she pays now. She is not a hard case. She is the ordinary case, and that is what should alarm us.

The Government's response has been to say that supply is the answer and that supply takes time. Supply is the answer in the long run, and I accept that no policy delivers a completed home in a quarter. But the people I have described do not live in the long run. They need protections now: a proper ban on no-fault evictions, rent controls that actually bind, and a functioning system of tenant purchase where a sitting tenant is not turned out simply because the landlord has spotted a better price.

And I say this to Ministers plainly. If the framework you have built cannot help a woman who has worked for twenty-two years and paid her rent every month, the framework is not merely under strain. It has failed at its purpose.

His third question was about the assumptions underlying the analysis. He is right that assumptions drive conclusions in exercises of this kind, and he is right to probe them. The analysis assumes no change in migration policy, no new trade agreements with third countries, and no mitigating domestic policy action. Each of those assumptions is, by construction, pessimistic, because each of them holds constant something that this Government fully intends to change. That is not a criticism of the analysts. It is simply what a baseline is.

Finally, he asked about publication in due course. My position is that when the work is complete, when the assumptions have been tested and when the modelling reflects the negotiated outcome rather than a hypothetical one, the House will see it. Parliament is entitled to the evidence on which decisions of this magnitude are taken, and I have no interest in withholding it.

The platforms have had a long time to demonstrate that self-regulation works, and the evidence before the Committee suggests that it has not. Material that is plainly unlawful remains accessible for hours and sometimes days after it is reported, and the reporting mechanisms themselves are frequently opaque, with no meaningful appeal and no explanation of the outcome.

I want to be careful here, because the question of speed cuts both ways. If we impose a duty to remove within a fixed and very short window, backed by significant penalties, the rational response of a platform is to over-remove. It will take down anything that has been reported, because the cost of a wrongful takedown falls on the user while the cost of a wrongful retention falls on the company. That is a real risk to legitimate speech, and those of us who want stronger regulation should not pretend otherwise.

The answer, I think, lies in process rather than in blunt deadlines. We should require platforms to have systems that are adequate to the volume and risk of the material they carry, to staff those systems properly rather than relying wholly on automated classification, to publish transparency data that can be independently audited, and to provide a genuine route of appeal for the user whose content is removed. A regulator should be assessing the adequacy of the system, not second-guessing every individual decision.

On the question of legislating, I say to the House that the threat of legislation is only credible if we are actually prepared to legislate. The industry has become skilled at announcing initiatives whenever a Bill is mentioned and allowing them to lapse when attention moves on. I would rather we set out clearly now what we expect, with a date attached, and made plain that the alternative is a statutory duty.

dogs are killed for human consumption every year, and a great many of them are stolen family pets, taken from gardens and from the ends of leads, transported in conditions that no one in this House would tolerate for any animal, and slaughtered by methods that are deliberately cruel because of a belief that fear improves the meat.

Members may reasonably ask why we need a law here, in this country, where the practice is vanishingly rare. Let me answer that directly. It is currently lawful in England and Wales to eat dog meat. The slaughter of a dog for meat is prohibited, and the sale of dog meat is prohibited, but the consumption of it is not, and neither is the possession of it where it has been obtained without a commercial sale. That is a gap. It is a small gap in practical terms, but it is a conspicuous one, and it undermines our ability to say anything credible to other Governments about their own trade.

That is the second reason. This country has, rightly, spent years pressing internationally on animal welfare, on the ivory trade, on live exports, on fur. When our diplomats raise the dog meat trade, they are met with the entirely fair observation that our own law does not close the loop. Closing it costs us nothing and removes the excuse.

The third reason is about theft. Dog theft has risen sharply, and the criminal networks involved are not sentimental about the purpose. A clear prohibition on possession for consumption gives enforcement authorities a straightforward offence to work with.

I want to be clear that this Bill is not directed at any community or any culture within our country. It is directed at a practice, and the practice has no defenders here. I commend the Bill to the House.

They cover health, education, housing, inequality, energy, water, industry and justice. A department whose expertise and mandate is international will inevitably approach the domestic review as an exercise in reporting rather than as an exercise in delivery, and reporting is not what the goals were designed to produce.

The Committee took evidence on this from a range of witnesses, and the point was made repeatedly that the countries which have done this well have placed the coordinating function at the centre, in the Cabinet Office or in the equivalent, with the authority to require contributions from departments and, crucially, with the authority to hold them to what they have contributed. Where the function has sat in a line department, the review has tended to become a compilation of existing announcements presented in a new order.

I also want to press the Secretary of State on the involvement of the devolved administrations and of local government. A great deal of what determines whether we meet goals on poverty, on housing quality and on public health is decided at local authority level, and local authorities have been almost entirely absent from the process so far. Several have adopted the goals in their own strategies, with real enthusiasm, and they have had almost no engagement from Whitehall in return.

Finally, on civil society. The review should be a moment of honest assessment, including of where we are going backwards, and that requires the participation of organisations who will say so. If the process is designed so that only comfortable evidence reaches the final document, we will produce something that reads well internationally and means nothing at home. I hope the Government will take these points in the constructive spirit in which the Committee offers them.

The subject of this debate is economic crime, and I want to make one central point. We have talked about this for a long time. There have been reports, reviews, consultations, action plans and strategies, and there has been a persistent gap between the diagnosis, which is largely agreed across this House, and the response, which is not. Everybody knows that our company registration regime allows a person to incorporate a company in this country in minutes, at a cost of twelve pounds, with no verification of who they are. Everybody knows that limited partnerships in certain jurisdictions of this country have been used at industrial scale for laundering. Everybody knows that our enforcement agencies are outgunned, out-resourced and out-lawyered by the people they are investigating.

On that last point I want to say something specific. Where an agency knows that losing a contested case may cost it a substantial share of its annual budget in adverse costs, it will not bring the case. That is not timidity. It is arithmetic. If we want enforcement, we have to change the arithmetic, whether through costs protection in the public interest or through proper resourcing, and preferably both.

There is also the matter of the enablers. The money does not launder itself. It moves through firms and advisers and agents who are regulated in this country, and the number of professional enablers who have faced serious consequences remains close to zero. Until that changes, the rest is decoration.

carried on division. This is a modest procedural change, but I want to explain why the Committee thought it necessary and why we recommend it to the House.

Under the existing practice, five members must rise to call for a recorded division. In a House where the smaller recognised parties do not always have five members present in the Chamber at the relevant moment, that requirement has the effect of denying those parties the ability to place their position formally on the record. In practice we have all seen the workaround: members of other parties rise in solidarity so that the threshold is reached. That is a courtesy, and it works most of the time, but it should not be a courtesy. A party's right to have its vote recorded should not depend on the goodwill of its opponents on a given afternoon.

The proposed change would allow one representative of a recognised party to request a recorded vote. It preserves the distinction between recognised parties and individual members, which the Committee thought important, because otherwise a single member could compel a recorded division on every question and the business of the House would slow to a crawl. It also preserves the alternative of simply indicating that a motion is carried on division, which allows a party to register dissent without the time cost of a full vote.

I want to acknowledge that some members have raised concerns about the effect on the length of sittings. The Committee considered that carefully and concluded that the effect is likely to be small, and that in any event the recording of votes is a core function of this place. Citizens are entitled to know how their member voted, and procedural thresholds designed for a different composition of the House should not stand in the way of that.

A teacher assigned to an ASD class without specific training is being asked to do skilled clinical work on the basis of general professional goodwill, and it is unfair to that teacher, unfair to the special needs assistants working alongside them, and above all unfair to the children.

The training pathway at the moment is fragmented. There are postgraduate courses, there are in-service modules, there are supports from the National Council for Special Education, and there are excellent teachers who have essentially trained themselves in the evenings because they cared enough to do it. What there is not is a coherent, funded, expected route that a teacher can enter knowing that the time will be released, the fees will be met and the qualification will be recognised in their career progression. Until that exists, we will continue to see ASD classes staffed by whoever is available in August.

I would also make a point about retention. Where teachers do acquire the specialist skills, they are often the first to be moved when a mainstream vacancy arises, because the school has to cover the timetable. The expertise walks out of the room. Some mechanism to protect specialist posts, and to recognise them in allowances or in promotion, would help.

The third element is continuity for the child. A child with autism who has spent a year building a relationship with a particular adult should not lose that relationship because a temporary contract has expired. The churn in this area is very high, and the cost of it is measured in regression that takes months to recover.

So I ask the Minister to look at training, at retention and at continuity together, because addressing one without the others will not work.

That message is harder to deliver now than it was a month ago, because the independent media inside Russia has been closed down, journalists have been driven into exile, and the criminal law has been amended so that describing the war accurately carries a fifteen-year sentence. Will the Government revisit it?

Second, visas and safe routes for Russians fleeing conscription and persecution. There is a genuine tension here, and I acknowledge the security concerns, but a blanket approach that treats every Russian passport holder as a proxy for their Government hands Putin exactly the narrative he wants.

Third, the design of the sanctions themselves. Sanctions that fall on oligarchs, on the central bank, on the defence industrial base and on the technology imports that sustain the war machine are proportionate and they are effective. Sanctions that simply raise the price of bread in Novosibirsk are neither. The evidence from other sanctions regimes is that broad measures against a population tend to consolidate support for the regime rather than erode it.

We should hold both thoughts at once. This war must fail, and it must be seen to fail. And the Russia that comes after Putin, whenever that is, should have reason to remember that we distinguished between a Government and a people.

To spend a weekend rightly celebrating the importance of talking about mental health, and then to discover that the very organisation involved is bound into an arrangement whose entire commercial logic depends on people gambling more, is a contradiction that will not have escaped anyone watching.

Let me set out the Government's position. We are conducting a review of gambling legislation, and it is a genuinely comprehensive one. The Gambling Act was passed before the smartphone existed. It was written for a world of betting shops and casinos, where the friction of leaving the house imposed a natural limit on how much harm a person could do to themselves in an evening. That friction is gone. A person can now lose a year's savings between the hours of two and four in the morning, alone, with no one to notice, and the product is designed by people who understand the psychology of that better than any regulator currently does.

Within that review we are looking specifically at advertising and at sponsorship, including sponsorship in sport, and including the arrangements the honourable Member has described. I am not going to pre-empt the outcome from this Dispatch Box, because a review that announces its conclusions before it has considered the evidence is not a review. But I will say that the honourable Member should not read our silence as indifference.

I also want to make a point about affordability checks and about data. The operators know precisely which customers are generating the losses. They know the pattern of behaviour that precedes a catastrophic loss, because they model it. The idea that they cannot identify a customer in trouble is not credible, and any regulatory framework worth the name must place that duty where the knowledge already sits.

The State's position was that the works were within scope. The court did not fully resolve the underlying question, and the matter was ultimately settled, which means that the public has paid twelve million euro more than the tender price without any public determination of who was at fault.

That is the pattern, and it is the pattern that concerns me far more than any single project. We tender competitively. The lowest compliant bid wins. The bid is priced on the assumption that variations will follow, because the bidder has read the same site investigation that we have and knows it is thin. The variations duly arrive. The final cost bears little relationship to the tender. And when anybody asks a question about it, we are told that the matter is commercially sensitive or subject to legal proceedings.

I want to ask the witnesses three things. First, at what point did the contracting authority know that the outturn would exceed the tender by more than twenty per cent, and was that communicated to the Department at the time or only afterwards? Second, what site investigation was carried out before the tender was issued, and who signed off on its adequacy? Third, has any lesson from this project been embedded in the procurement guidance for subsequent projects, and can we see the document in which that was done?

I make no allegation of impropriety against anyone. I do allege that we have a systemic problem in which the tendered price of a public project has become a work of fiction, and that we keep discovering this afresh on each project as though it had never happened before.

We have taken action, and the results are measurable. Prices for wireless services have come down substantially over the period, and they have come down fastest in the plans that ordinary families actually buy.

But let me be direct with the member, because I do not think the exchange of statistics across this floor is what Canadians want to hear. They want to know why their bill is still higher than the bill of somebody in a comparable country. And the honest answer is that the geography of this country is genuinely difficult, that serving a community of four hundred people three hundred kilometres from the nearest fibre backbone is genuinely expensive, and that none of that fully explains the gap. Some of the gap is market structure, and market structure is something government can change.

That is why we have pursued a policy of supporting regional carriers, why we imposed conditions on the transaction the member mentions rather than approving it as submitted, and why we have set clear expectations of the incumbents with respect to wholesale access. Where those expectations are not met, further action is available to us and we will not hesitate to use it.

I would also say to the member that connectivity is not only about price. It is about whether the service exists at all. There are communities in my own province and in his where the question is not the cost of the plan but whether there is a signal on the highway when a family is in trouble. That is where a substantial share of our investment has gone, and I make no apology for it.

Madeleine trained at a time when nursing offered women limited authority and considerable responsibility, and she made the most of both. She worked night shifts through the years when her own children were small. She took on the cases other people found difficult, the patients who were frightened or angry or alone, and she stayed with them. Those who worked alongside her tell me that she had a particular gift for treating a person in a hospital bed as a person rather than as a condition, and that in a profession under constant pressure this is harder than it sounds and rarer than it should be.

When she retired from nursing she did not retire from work. She volunteered at the parish, she organized the meal program that still runs today, and she became an advocate for seniors in her neighbourhood who were struggling to navigate benefits and housing. She would arrive at my constituency office with a folder and a list, and she was not easily satisfied, and I say that with the greatest affection. She understood that advocacy is not a matter of expressing concern. It is a matter of returning until something changes.

Madeleine passed away last month, surrounded by her family, at the age of ninety-one. She leaves four children, eleven grandchildren and a community that is measurably kinder for her having been in it.

To her family I offer my condolences, and my gratitude. Let us do what needs to be done. We could do worse, all of us in this place, than to take that as our own instruction.

They are not a policy in themselves, and a strategy that consists solely of tightening pressure while closing every channel of communication has a predictable destination, and it is not one that anybody in this House wants to reach.

I would make three observations. The first is about the nuclear file specifically. Whatever criticisms may fairly be made of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, and there were legitimate ones about sunset clauses and about the exclusion of missile development, it did what it was designed to do: it lengthened the breakout time and it put inspectors on the ground. Since it collapsed, enrichment has advanced and monitoring has been curtailed. That is a worse position by any measure. Rebuilding something on that ground is difficult, but it is not impossible, and it requires that somebody is talking.

The second is about regional actors. Any durable arrangement has to involve the Gulf states, and the recent thaw between Riyadh and Tehran, whatever one thinks of how it was brokered, creates an opening that we should be working actively rather than observing.

The third is about the Iranian people. We should not confuse a Government with a nation. The protests of recent months, and the extraordinary courage of the women leading them, remind us that there is a society there with its own trajectory. Our sanctions should target the security apparatus and the individuals responsible for repression, and they should avoid, so far as they can, the medicines and the basic goods that hurt ordinary families and give the regime a grievance to broadcast.

So yes to pressure, calibrated and targeted. But the door stays open, because a closed door leads to only one place.

The substance of my argument is straightforward. The Sewel convention states that this Parliament will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the Scottish Parliament. The word normally was always understood to describe an exception, something rare and justified. In practice, over the last several years, consent has been refused and legislation has proceeded on a number of occasions, and the exception has begun to look like a routine.

I am not arguing that the convention should be converted into a veto. I understand why a sovereign Parliament will not bind itself in that way, and I accept the constitutional logic. What I am arguing is that if consent can be overridden at will and without consequence, then it is not consent, and we should stop describing it as such. At minimum, there should be a requirement that where the Government proceeds without consent, a Minister comes to this House, sets out the reasons, and submits to questioning on them. That is not a radical proposition. It is what we would expect for any other constitutional convention we claimed to respect.

The second point concerns common frameworks. A great deal of work was done, quietly and constructively, by officials in all four administrations to develop frameworks in the areas returning from Brussels. There is a difference between a world that is two degrees warmer, which is difficult and expensive and survivable with serious planning, and a world in which the permafrost releases what it is holding and the West Antarctic ice sheet passes the point of recovery. The first is a policy problem. The second is not a problem at all, because problems have solutions.

A Government that funds adaptation while missing its mitigation targets is buying umbrellas while raising the sea level.

On adaptation specifically, I would make one point that I think is underappreciated here. Our adaptation planning is heavily weighted towards flood defence, for understandable reasons. But the risks to this country over the coming decades include water scarcity in the east, changes in the growing season that will affect what agriculture can do, the arrival of vector-borne disease, and heat in a building stock designed exclusively to retain it. The honourable Member's argument, as I understood it, was that the companies operating in the North Sea have extracted enormous value, paid too little tax, and should now be compelled to fund the transition. I want to engage with that seriously, because parts of it are right and parts of it are not.

What is right is that the fiscal regime has been repeatedly redesigned, and that the redesigns have generally been favourable to the operators at moments when the price environment did not require it. The decommissioning relief arrangements in particular mean that the taxpayer will meet a substantial share of the cost of removing infrastructure whose profits were privately retained. That is a legitimate criticism and I have made it myself.

What I think is wrong is the characterisation of the workforce. There are around two hundred thousand people whose livelihoods depend on this industry across the United Kingdom, and a very large proportion of them are in Aberdeen and the north east of Scotland. They are welders, ROV pilots, subsea engineers, geoscientists, helicopter crews, caterers. They are not the people who set the tax rates or the dividend policy, and when the debate in this Chamber slides from criticising the companies to treating the industry as something shameful, those people hear it.

They also happen to be the people who will build the offshore wind, the carbon capture and the hydrogen infrastructure, because the skills transfer almost directly. Every one of them who leaves for the Gulf or for Australia is a skill we will have to import later. That is the practical case for a managed transition rather than an abrupt one, and it is the case the Government has, at best, half made.

We heard about the languages that were beaten out of children and the families that were broken and the generations that inherited the consequences. And then the commission produced ninety-four calls to action, in plain language, with numbers on them, so that nobody could ever say afterwards that they did not know what was being asked.

My critique is this. In this chamber we have become fluent in the vocabulary of reconciliation and considerably less fluent in the practice of it. We say the words. We do the acknowledgment. And then we vote on estimates that do not fund the things the calls to action require, and we defend in court the very cases that a reconciled relationship would settle, and we ask survivors to prove again what they have already testified to.

Let me take one example. Call to action number one concerns the number of indigenous children in care. It is the first one for a reason. The residential school system took children from their families, and the child welfare system continues to take children from their families, in numbers that exceed the peak of the residential school era. A person could be forgiven for concluding that the institution changed and the practice did not.

Or take clean drinking water. It is not among the ninety-four calls, but it is the most basic test of whether a government's stated commitments mean anything, and the long-term advisories persist in communities that have been waiting for decades.

I am not standing here to say that nothing has been done. Things have been done, by this government and by others, and I acknowledge them. What I am saying is that survivors did not testify so that we could hold a ceremony. They testified so that something would change, and the pace of change is not something any of us should be comfortable defending.
